Topic: Why should any man be taxed to support a government he never consented to, and called a rebel the moment he objects?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
Consent is not a document men sign; it is a condition they either possess the arms to enforce or do not. To ask why one should be taxed without consent is to mistake law's parchment origin for its true foundation, which is force sufficient to compel obedience and generosity enough to make obedience tolerable.

A prince who taxes must do two things at once: extract enough to arm himself against every rival, and extract little enough that the extracted do not conclude rebellion costs less than payment. "Rebel" is simply the name power gives to refusal it has not yet crushed or bought — the label carries no moral content, only a report on who currently holds the field. Your grievance is real, but it is not an argument against taxation; it is evidence that this prince has not yet made you fear him or love him enough, and one of those two he must urgently correct.

The complaint is just; the remedy is not petition but leverage — consent follows power, it does not summon it.

*He who cannot be refused is never called a tyrant; he who can be refused and is not, was never truly ruled at all.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
Every man who cries "consent" imagines himself in that pristine moment before the Commonwealth, weighing terms as a free agent. He is not. He is already inside the artifice he pretends to judge, alive only because the Sword has kept his neighbour's knife from his throat.

Consent was never a signature — it is the standing fact that you have not returned to the war of all against all. The instant you call the sovereign's tax illegitimate while still sheltering under his peace, you have already consented in the only coin that matters: your continued obedience. What you resent is not the absence of consent but the presence of obligation, and no covenant survives men who reserve the right to unmake it whenever it costs them something.

The man who objects while still protected has not been wronged — he has been caught wanting the peace without its price.

*He who enjoys the peace consents to its cost; the rebel is merely the man who forgot he ever feared the alternative.*
Keynes — Judgement:
The question of consent and taxation strikes at the very root of what binds a citizen to the state — and it presumes a false picture of what the state is for.

Consent given once, by men long dead, cannot obligate the living any more than a contract can bind those who never signed it — but that is precisely why we should abandon consent as the test altogether. The state is not a club one joins by signature; it is the vehicle through which a community deliberately manages the demand, employment, and stability that no individual, however sovereign in theory, can secure alone. The rebel who refuses taxation on grounds of unconsent imagines himself self-sufficient in a world where his very prosperity depends on collective management he did not personally author.

Taxation needs no signature — it needs only that the state, in return, actually govern well.

*The state that spends wisely earns its keep; the state that governs badly earns its rebels — consent was never the real question.*
Hayek — Judgement:
Taxation without consent is the archetype of coercion dressed as necessity — the majority's rule imposed on the individual, who is then branded a criminal for noticing the imposition.

But my quarrel was never with taxation as such — some coercion is unavoidable if we're to have a Rule of Law that itself constrains power. The real question is whether the taxing authority is bound by general, known rules applied equally to all, or whether it wields arbitrary discretion in the name of some collective plan. Consent is a fiction in any large society; what matters is whether power is predictable, limited, and blind to persons. A government that taxes under law, and can be resisted through law, differs categorically from one that taxes by decree and calls dissent treason.

The wrong is not being taxed without a signature — it's being taxed by an authority that recognizes no rule higher than its own will.

*The rebel is not the man who refuses to pay — he is the first to notice the ruler has stopped obeying the law himself.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
Taxation without consent is not an administrative inconvenience but the precise mechanism by which one portion of mankind is reduced to legislate for another—the same logic by which women, having no voice in the laws, are pronounced content with their chains. I have always held that no man, and no woman, owes obedience to authority reason has not examined and consent has not ratified; a government that taxes the unrepresented does not persuade them of its justice, it merely spares itself the trouble of proving it. To call the objector a rebel is the oldest trick of unearned power: it converts a demand for reason into a crime against order, so that the man who asks *why* is punished before the man who commands is ever asked to justify himself. Consent, not birth or fear, is the only lawful hinge of obligation, and a government resting on the other is a tyranny wearing the mask of custom.

*Obedience without consent is not citizenship but servitude with better manners.*
